objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how each main system in your training airplane works, spot the signs that one is failing, take the right first steps, and run the checklists that operate those systems.
why: Engines, fuel, electrics and instruments rarely fail without warning. A pilot who knows what normal looks like catches trouble early, while there is still time and altitude to fix it.

prereading.what: Primary and secondary flight controls, trim, autopilot basics
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 6, 6-1 to 6-12

prereading.what: Engine, prop, induction and carb ice, ignition, oil, fuel, electrical, hydraulic, gear, heat, oxygen, ice protection. Skip turbine engine pages 7-20 to 7-25.
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 7, 7-1 to 7-41

prereading.what: Pitot-static instruments, blockages, glass displays, vacuum and gyro instruments
prereading.label: PHAK Ch 8, 8-1 to 8-22

prereading.what: Electrical fire, flap and elevator failures, gear, electrical and pitot-static malfunctions, abnormal engine indications
prereading.label: AFH Ch 18, 18-10 to 18-16

prereading.what: Ice protection on airplanes NOT certified for icing
prereading.label: AC 91-74B para 3-13 to 3-15

warmup: You are cruising at night and the panel lights slowly get dimmer. Which system is failing, how much time do you have, and what would you turn off first?

key_terms.def: Ailerons, elevator (or stabilator) and rudder. Needed to control the airplane.
Flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers and trim. They improve performance or ease control forces.
Small hinged tab on a control surface that holds the surface where you want it, so you don't have to.
Ice that forms in the carburetor venturi and throttle valve from fuel vaporization and pressure drop. It chokes the engine.
Engine-driven generator that makes the spark. Works without the airplane's electrical system.
Gauges that show whether the alternator is charging the battery and how much load it carries.
A common connection point that feeds electrical power to the equipment.
Ram air (pitot) and outside air pressure (static) lines that run the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI.
Engine-driven pump that spins the gyros in the attitude and heading indicators in many trainers.
Anti-ice prevents ice from forming. Deice removes ice that has already formed.
Attitude and Heading Reference System and Air Data Computer: the sensors behind a glass-cockpit display.

body.p: The ailerons, elevator (or stabilator) and rudder are the primary flight controls. You need them to control the airplane safely. [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]]

bullets: Ailerons move opposite each other. Right yoke: right aileron up, left aileron down, airplane rolls right. [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]
Adverse yaw: the down aileron makes more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn. Rudder fixes it. [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]
Pulling back raises the elevator trailing edge, the tail goes down and the nose goes up. [[1:153|PHAK 6-5]]
A stabilator is a one-piece tail that pivots. An antiservo tab makes it less sensitive. [[1:155|PHAK 6-7]]
Left pedal moves the rudder left and yaws the nose left. The rudder gets more effective with speed. [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]

body.p: Controls feel soft and sluggish at low airspeed and firm at high airspeed. Control stops limit travel so you don't overstress the airplane. [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]

callout.text: Preflight: move every control through its full range in all directions. AFH says pilots often don't, and that is not acceptable. [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]

check.q: Which control surface moves the airplane about the lateral axis?
check.a: The elevator (or stabilator). It controls pitch. [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]]

chunks.title: Secondary flight controls: flaps and trim

body.p: Flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers and trim are the secondary controls. They improve performance or take control pressure off the pilot. [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]]

Flaps on the trailing edge increase both lift and induced drag at any angle of attack. They allow a low landing speed while keeping a fast cruise, because you extend them only when needed. [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]

bullets: Plain flap: simplest, adds camber, lots of drag, nose-down pitch. [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]]
Slotted flap: most popular today. A slot feeds fast air over the flap for much more lift. [[1:156|PHAK 6-8]] [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]]
Fowler flap: slides back on tracks. Early travel adds lots of lift and little drag; last part adds mostly drag. [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]]
Flap extension can pitch the nose up or down depending on the airplane. Retrim. [[1:157|PHAK 6-9]]

body.p: Trim tabs relieve constant pressure. On most small airplanes a trim wheel moves a tab on the elevator. The tab moves opposite to the elevator: nose-down trim moves the tab up, which pushes the elevator down. [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]

callout.text: Set power, set pitch, set configuration, THEN trim. Change any of those and you trim again. [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]

body.p: Many small airplanes also have a fixed rudder tab that is bent on the ground. [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]

check.q: You are holding steady back pressure in a climb. What do you do?
check.a: Add nose-up trim until the pressure is gone. [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]

body.p: Most trainers have a four-stroke, spark-ignition, horizontally opposed engine. The four strokes are intake, compression, power and exhaust. [[1:162|PHAK 7-2]] [[1:163|PHAK 7-3]]
Ignition. Two magnetos each fire one of the two spark plugs in every cylinder. Magnetos make their own electricity, so they work even with the master switch off. [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]

bullets: Run-up mag check: BOTH to R, back to BOTH, then to L. A small rpm drop is normal; the POH lists the limit. [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]
Engine quits on one mag, or drop too big: don't fly. "No drop" is not normal either: don't fly. [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
After shutdown, ignition OFF. A hot mag can start the engine if someone moves the prop. [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]

body.p: Mixture. Air gets thinner as you climb but fuel does not, so the mixture gets richer. Lean it as you climb. Enrich it as you descend, or it may get too lean and cause detonation. [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]
Carburetor ice. Fuel vaporizing and the pressure drop in the venturi chill the air. Ice forms at the throttle valve and venturi and cuts power. [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]

head: Fact
Value
rows: Up to 100 °F (38 °C) and humidity as low as 50% [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]
Manifold pressure drops, RPM stays the same [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]

bullets: If ice is suspected: FULL carb heat and leave it on until power returns. Partial heat can make it worse. [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
With ice present, RPM drops more, then slowly rises as ice melts. The engine may run rough for 30 seconds to several minutes. [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Apply carb heat before closing the throttle for a descent. Ice is most dangerous at reduced power. [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Don't use carb heat when full power is needed, like takeoff, except to check for or remove ice. [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]]

callout.text: Fuel injection is less prone to icing, but impact ice can still block the air intake. The alternate air source fixes that. [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]] [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]

body.p: Detonation is explosive burning in the cylinder, shown by high cylinder head temperatures. Causes include too-low fuel grade, a too-lean mixture at high power, and long steep climbs. [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]]

check.q: In a fixed-pitch airplane, RPM slowly drops in cruise on a humid 60 °F day. What do you suspect and do?
check.a: Carburetor ice. Apply full carb heat and keep it on until power returns. [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]

head: Fixed-pitch prop
Constant-speed prop
rows: One airspeed/RPM combo; climb or cruise prop [[1:165|PHAK 7-5]]
A wide range; governor holds RPM [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]]

callout.text: Constant-speed prop: reducing power, take manifold pressure off first, then RPM. Adding power, RPM up first, then manifold pressure. [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]

body.p: Oil lubricates, cools, seals the pistons and carries away dirt. Engines use a wet-sump system (oil kept in a sump on the engine) or a dry-sump system (separate oil tank); dry sump suits very large engines. [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]

bullets: Oil pressure should rise during engine start. Green = normal, red = limits. [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Oil temperature changes slowly. High temp can mean low oil, a plugged line or a blocked cooler. [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]
Check oil quantity and type on every preflight. [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]

body.p: Cooling. Air cooling works poorly on the ground and in slow, high-power climbs. To cool a hot engine: more airspeed, richer mixture and/or less power. Open cowl flaps if you have them. [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]] [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]
The cylinder head temperature (CHT) gauge shows engine heat directly; oil temperature is a delayed sign. [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]

check.q: In a constant-speed prop airplane, what is the correct order to reduce power?
check.a: Reduce manifold pressure first, then RPM. [[1:167|PHAK 7-7]]

body.p: The fuel system must give the engine clean fuel without a break, in every approved attitude. High-wing trainers often use gravity feed. Low-wing airplanes need pumps: an engine-driven pump plus an electric boost pump for starting and backup. [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]

bullets: Selector: LEFT, RIGHT, BOTH, OFF on many airplanes. Obey placards like "BOTH for takeoff and landing." [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]
Running a tank dry can let air in and cause vapor lock, making a restart hard. [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]
Fuel gauges must only be accurate when they read empty. Always check tanks visually. [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]
Lock the primer. A loose primer can make the mixture too rich in flight. [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]
Tanks are vented. Fuel dripping from the overflow on a hot day can be normal. [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]

body.p: Colors from [[1:187|PHAK Fig 7-32]]. Never use a lower grade than required; the next higher grade is OK. Never use auto gas unless the airplane has an STC for it. [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]

callout.text: Drain the strainer and every tank sump before each flight. If you find water, keep draining until none shows. Never take off with water or dirt in the fuel. [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]] [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]

check.q: Your fuel gauge reads half full. Is that good enough for preflight?
check.a: No. Gauges only need to be accurate at empty. Check each tank visually. [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]

body.p: Most airplanes have a 14- or 28-volt DC system. Parts: alternator or generator, battery, master switch, alternator switch, bus bar, fuses and circuit breakers, voltage regulator, ammeter or loadmeter, and wiring. [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]

bullets: The engine-driven alternator powers the system and charges the battery. The battery starts the engine and is a short backup. [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]
Master ON powers everything except ignition. Magnetos don't need it. [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]
Split master: left half ALT, right half BAT. ALT off puts the whole load on the battery. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Circuit breakers protect circuits from overload and can be reset; fuses must be replaced. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
The bus bar is the common point that feeds power to the equipment. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

head: Ammeter shows
Meaning
rows: More current leaving the battery than going in [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

body.p: A loadmeter starts at zero and shows the load on the alternator. Some airplanes have only a low-voltage warning light. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

callout.text: After start, know your normal gauges and sounds. Low voltage, high ammeter or loadmeter readings, dimming lights or radio noise can mean the starter is still running (stuck relay). Shut the engine down and don't fly until it is fixed. [[18:1|AC 91-55A]]

check.q: The ammeter shows a full-scale minus reading. What has probably failed?

body.p: In small airplanes, hydraulics usually run the wheel brakes, and sometimes retractable gear and constant-speed props. A basic system has a reservoir, pump, filter, selector valve, relief valve and actuator. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]] Use only the fluid type the manufacturer specifies. [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]]

head: Gear type
Key points
rows: Harder braking without nosing over, better view, resists ground loops because the CG is ahead of the mains [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]]
CG behind the mains, so harder to control on the ground; can ground loop; needs specific training [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]]
Less drag; electric or hydraulic; position lights, warning horn, emergency extension [[24:243|AFH 12-12]] [[24:245|AFH 12-14]]

bullets: Steerable nosewheels link to the rudder pedals; castering nosewheels may need differential braking. [[1:193|PHAK 7-33]]
Toe brakes work separately for differential braking. [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]]

Retractable gear: gear warning horn sounds when configured to land with gear not down and locked. A squat switch prevents retraction with weight on the wheels. [[24:243|AFH 12-12]] [[24:245|AFH 12-14]]

check.q: Why does a tailwheel airplane tend to ground loop?
check.a: Its CG is behind the main wheels, so a swerve tends to grow. [[1:194|PHAK 7-34]]

body.p: The pitot tube feeds ram (total) pressure only to the airspeed indicator. The static port feeds outside air pressure to the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI. [[1:203|PHAK 8-1]] [[1:204|PHAK 8-2]]

bullets: Preflight: remove the pitot cover and check that the pitot opening, drain hole and static ports are clear. [[1:204|PHAK 8-2]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
Altimeter check: set the current altimeter setting. If it is off more than 75 feet from field elevation, it needs repair. [[1:209|PHAK 8-7]]
VSI should read near zero on the ground. [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]
Pitot heat protects against ice in visible moisture. [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]

head: Blockage
What you see
rows: Airspeed acts like an altimeter: rises in a climb, falls in a descent [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Altimeter freezes, VSI stays at zero, airspeed reads low above and high below the blockage altitude [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]

body.p: Fix for a static blockage: open the alternate static source. Because cabin pressure is lower, the altimeter reads a bit high, airspeed reads high, and the VSI shows a brief climb. [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]

callout.text: No alternate static? Breaking the VSI glass lets cabin air into the static lines. The VSI is the least important static instrument. [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]

check.q: In a climb, the altimeter stops moving and the VSI shows zero. What is blocked, and what is your fix?
check.a: The static system. Open the alternate static source. [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]] [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]

body.p: In many trainers an engine-driven vacuum pump spins the attitude and heading indicator gyros, and the electrical system powers the turn coordinator. Two power sources mean you keep some bank information if one fails. [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]

bullets: Normal suction is usually between 4.5 "Hg and 5.5 "Hg. Check your POH. [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]
Low suction: the attitude and heading indicators may become unstable and wrong. Some airplanes have a low-vacuum light. [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]
The heading indicator drifts. Reset it to the magnetic compass about every 15 minutes in straight, level, steady flight. [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]
Turn coordinator: the second mark shows a standard-rate turn, 3° per second. It shows rate and direction of turn only, not bank angle or pitch. [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]] [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]
Taxi check: turn needle shows the turn, ball moves opposite, heading indicator turns correctly. [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]] [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]

callout.text: A failing vacuum pump does not shout. The attitude indicator slowly tips or drifts. Cross-check the turn coordinator, heading and altimeter, and glance at the suction gauge. [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]] [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]

check.q: Which instrument still gives bank information if the vacuum pump fails in a typical trainer?

chunks.title: Avionics, glass displays and the autopilot

body.p: Glass cockpits show the basic flight instruments on one primary flight display (PFD). PHAK counts the tachometer as the one "six pack" instrument not on the PFD; it usually goes on the multi-function display (MFD). If a screen fails, it is shown on the remaining screen with the flight instruments. [[1:214|PHAK 8-12]] [[1:215|PHAK 8-13]]

bullets: The Air Data Computer (ADC) turns pitot and static pressure into airspeed and altitude. [[1:216|PHAK 8-14]]
The AHRS gives attitude; a magnetometer gives heading. AHRS doesn't tumble like old gyros. [[1:215|PHAK 8-13]] [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]]
Magenta trend vectors show where airspeed and altitude will be in 6 seconds. [[1:216|PHAK 8-14]]
Autopilot: holds heading and altitude. Single-axis = ailerons only; three-axis = ailerons, elevator, rudder. It has a disconnect and can be overridden. [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]

body.p: Managing automation (R3). Always know which autopilot modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify armed modes engage when they should. On some systems, switching the HSI from GPS to VOR while in NAV mode drops the autopilot to ROL (wings level). [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]

callout.text: Humans are poor monitors of automation. The more reliable it is, the worse we watch it. Double-check programming, make callouts, and stay ready to hand-fly. [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]] If automation misbehaves, disconnect it and fly the airplane. [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]

check.q: You change the HSI source from GPS to VOR with the autopilot in NAV mode, and the airplane stops tracking. Why?
check.a: On some autopilots, that change disengages NAV mode and reverts to ROL (wings level). Re-engage NAV. [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]

chunks.title: Environmental systems: heat, CO and pressurization

body.p: Most light airplanes heat the cabin with a shroud around the muffler. Outside air is warmed there and ducted to the cabin and windshield defrost. [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]

callout.text: Exhaust has carbon monoxide (CO): colorless and odorless. A cracked muffler can leak CO into the heat. [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]] Signs: headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness, weakness. Action: heater OFF, fresh air vents and windows open, oxygen if you have it. [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]

bullets: Cheap CO detectors change color when CO is present. [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
Larger airplanes may use combustion heaters that burn aircraft fuel; they have an overheat switch that shuts off fuel. [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]] [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]
Pressurized airplanes usually keep cabin altitude near 8,000 feet at max cruise altitude. The main danger of losing pressure is hypoxia. [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]

check.q: You smell exhaust with the cabin heat on. What do you do?
check.a: Assume CO. Heater off, open fresh air vents and windows, use oxygen if available, and land. [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]

body.p: Anti-ice prevents ice from forming. Deice removes ice that already formed. [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]

head: System
Type
How to use
rows: Preheats intake air; best used as prevention [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Inflate to crack ice off. FAA recommends cycling at the first sign of ice [[38:23|AC 91-74B p.19]] [[38:24|AC 91-74B p.20]]
Turn on BEFORE entering icing [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]] [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]] [[38:25|AC 91-74B p.21]]
Check on preflight; one dead boot can cause severe vibration [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]

callout.text: Most light airplanes have only pitot heat and are NOT certified for icing. If you pick up ice, exit immediately. [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]] Even boots on a non-certified airplane are for emergency exit only: performance is unknown, stall warning may not work, and controls may jam. [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]] [[38:33|AC 91-74B 3-13]]

bullets: Ice on the wing can make it stall before the stall warning sounds. Maintain airspeed and watch angle of attack. [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11]]
An electrically heated windshield can cause compass deviation of as much as 40°. [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]

check.q: You are in a non-icing-certified airplane and see ice on the wing strut. What now?
check.a: Pitot heat on and exit the icing conditions immediately. Maintain airspeed, because the wing can stall before the stall warning sounds. [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]] [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11]]

head: Cabin pressure altitude
Rule (14 CFR 91.211)
rows: Above 12,500 ft MSL up to and including 14,000 ft MSL
Required minimum flight crew must have and use oxygen for the part of the flight at these altitudes that lasts more than 30 minutes
Required minimum flight crew must have and use oxygen the entire time at these altitudes
Each occupant must be provided with oxygen (they don't have to use it)

body.p: Source: [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. FAA recommends oxygen above 10,000 feet in the day and above 5,000 feet at night. [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]

bullets: Oxygen is stored at 1,800 to 2,200 psi. Cold makes the gauge read lower. [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Types: cannula, diluter-demand, pressure-demand, continuous-flow and pulse-demand. Systems certified above 18,000 feet need masks, not cannulas. [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]]
Fire danger: no oil or grease near oxygen, and no smoking. [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
Preflight: check quantity, mask and tubing, regulator, flow indicators. Shut everything off after use. [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]
A pulse oximeter shows your blood oxygen so you can judge your real need. [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]]

callout.text: Hypoxia can start with euphoria and a false sense that all is fine. At 25,000 feet, time of useful consciousness is only 3 to 5 minutes. [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]

check.q: You will cruise at 13,500 ft MSL for 45 minutes. Must you use oxygen?
check.a: Yes, for the time beyond 30 minutes at that altitude. [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]

body.p: Detecting a failure (R1) starts with knowing normal. Scan the engine and electrical gauges and cross-check flight instruments. Managing it (R2) means: keep flying the airplane, then follow the POH checklist, then decide where to land. A malfunction that pulls your attention away from flying can cause loss of control. [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] The manufacturer's procedures take precedence over general guidance. [[24:372|AFH 18-23]]

head: Malfunction
Likely cause
First action
rows: Carb/induction ice or clogged air filter
Low oil, failed relief valve, bad bearings
Poor cooling, oil congealed in cooler, detonation, coming engine failure
Reduce power, add airspeed; land as soon as possible if it continues
Cowl flaps, low airspeed, lean mixture, detonation
More airspeed, richer mixture, less power
Shed load; land as soon as practicable
Engine pump failed or no fuel

body.p: Table summarized from [[24:365|AFH Fig 18-11]]. Your POH procedures come first.

Electrical failure. Most failures are the alternator. The battery may last only minutes: a 40-amp load might drain it in about 10 or 15 minutes. Shed non-essential loads right away and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport. Electric flaps and gear may not work on a weak battery, so expect a no-flap landing. [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]
Electrical fire. First sign is usually the smell of burning insulation. Find and isolate the circuit; if you can't, turn off the master and alternator. Land as soon as possible. [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]

Pitot-static. A partly blocked static source may look normal until you descend. Then the instruments say you are too high, too fast and descending too slowly. Confirm by opening alternate static while climbing or descending. [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]

bullets: No flaps: landing distance can be as much as 50 percent longer. Fly a wider pattern; don't dive. [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Split flap: sharp roll toward the wing with less flap. Use opposite aileron and rudder; land faster than normal. [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Elevator cable failure: trim can still give limited pitch control. [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Gear won't extend: use the POH alternate method; if still stuck, choose an airport with rescue equipment. [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]

callout.text: Aviate, then diagnose, then checklist, then land. Don't let a failure take your eyes off flying the airplane.

check.q: Your alternator fails at night, 30 minutes from home. What are your first steps?
check.a: Shed all non-essential electrical load, tell ATC, and land at the nearest suitable airport. Expect no electric flaps. [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]

chunks.title: Operating systems and using checklists on the checkride

body.p: The examiner will have you operate at least three systems and use the right checklists. Know where each control is and what normal looks like in YOUR airplane.

bullets: Before takeoff, most airplanes check: fuel selector, trim set, full and free controls, mags and carb heat, prop (if constant-speed), electrical charging, vacuum, instruments and avionics. [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Typical vacuum: 4.8 to 5.2 "Hg at 2,000 rpm; use your POH value. [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Shutdown: check mag grounding at idle, mixture idle cutoff, then mags and master off. [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]

body.p: A checklist is a memory aid, not just a "do list." You may do the items and then use the checklist to confirm them. What matters is using it every time. [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]

check.q: Name the phases where you should use a prepared checklist.
check.a: Preflight, before start, start, before taxi, before takeoff, after takeoff, cruise, descent, before landing, after landing, and shutdown. [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]

scenario.title: Night trip home with a dying alternator
scenario.setup: You are flying a glass-cockpit trainer home at night, 40 minutes out, autopilot in NAV mode on a GPS route. You notice the ammeter is showing a discharge and, a minute later, the low-voltage light comes on. While looking at the electrical page you switch the HSI to VOR to check your position, and a few minutes later you notice the heading is drifting off course.

questions.q: What told you there was a problem, and what does it mean?
questions.a: An ammeter discharge and a low-voltage light point to an alternator/generator failure. The battery is now carrying the whole load. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]] [[24:365|AFH Fig 18-11]]

questions.q: How long can the battery last?
questions.a: It depends on the load and battery condition. AFH notes a 40-amp load might drain a battery in about 10 or 15 minutes. Act now. [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]
Keep flying the airplane. Run the POH checklist, shed non-essential loads, tell ATC, and divert to the nearest suitable airport instead of pressing home. [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]

questions.q: Why is the airplane drifting off course?
questions.a: On some autopilots, changing the nav source from GPS to VOR while in NAV mode drops the autopilot to ROL (wings level). You must know which modes are engaged and armed and verify what the automation is doing. [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]

questions.q: What should you expect on landing?
questions.a: Electric flaps (and gear) may not work on a weak battery. Plan a no-flap landing with a longer, wider pattern and more runway. [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]

skills.do: Operate at least three systems correctly, for example: fuel selector and boost pump, carburetor heat and mixture, flaps and trim, electrical switches and avionics, pitot heat, alternate static or alternate air. Explain what each does as you use it.
skills.practice: Sit in the airplane with the POH and touch each control while saying what it does and what normal indications look like. Practice the run-up with your CFI until you can explain every gauge.

skills.do: Use the appropriate POH checklists (preflight, start, run-up, before takeoff, cruise, descent, landing, shutdown, and emergency/abnormal) at the right times.
skills.practice: Chair-fly whole flights with the checklist in hand. Have your CFI call out failures (alternator, low oil pressure, carb ice) and find and run the right checklist.

quiz.q: Which of these are secondary flight controls?
quiz.why: Flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers and trim are secondary controls. [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]]

quiz.q: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, carburetor ice first shows up as:
options: A drop in manifold pressure with no RPM change
quiz.why: The governor holds RPM, so the loss of power shows as a drop in manifold pressure. [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]

quiz.q: During the mag check, there is no RPM drop at all on one magneto. You should:
options: Fly; it means the mag is perfect
Not fly; no drop is not normal
quiz.why: PHAK says "no drop" is not normal and the airplane should not be flown. [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]

quiz.q: A full-scale minus deflection on the ammeter indicates:
quiz.why: Full-scale minus = alternator/generator problem; full-scale plus = regulator problem. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

quiz.q: If the static port is blocked, which is TRUE?
options: Only the airspeed indicator is affected
The VSI shows a constant climb
The altimeter freezes and the VSI reads zero
quiz.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter and leaves the VSI at zero. [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]

quiz.q: Using the cabin alternate static source usually makes the altimeter read:
quiz.why: Cabin pressure is lower than outside, so the altimeter reads slightly high and airspeed reads high. [[1:205|PHAK 8-3]]

quiz.q: What normally powers the attitude and heading indicators in a vacuum-equipped trainer?
quiz.why: A vane-type engine-driven vacuum pump spins the gyros. [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]

quiz.q: Above what cabin pressure altitude must every occupant be provided supplemental oxygen?
quiz.why: 14 CFR 91.211(a)(3): above 15,000 feet MSL each occupant must be provided oxygen. [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]

quiz.q: Your airplane is not certified for icing and you pick up ice. The FAA recommends:
options: Exit icing conditions as quickly as possible
quiz.why: Airplanes not certificated for icing should exit icing conditions as expeditiously as possible. [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13]]

quiz.q: After an alternator failure, why might electric flaps be a problem?
options: Flaps are powered by the magnetos
Flap motors use lots of power and may drain a weak battery
Flaps only work with the autopilot
quiz.why: Gear and flap motors use power much faster than most equipment; selecting them on a partly drained battery can cause total power loss. [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]

takeaways: Know what normal looks like on every gauge, so abnormal jumps out.
Carb ice: full heat, leave it on until power comes back.
Alternator failure: shed load, land at the nearest suitable airport, expect no electric flaps.
Static blocked: altimeter freezes, VSI zero; open alternate static.
Vacuum failure: attitude and heading lie; trust the turn coordinator and cross-check.
Fly the airplane first, then run the checklist, and know which autopilot modes are on.
cfi_notes: K1 has twelve sub-elements; if the examiner selects K1, they must test at least three of them. Prepare the student for all of them, especially on the specific training airplane and its POH.
Students often mix up which instruments use pitot vs static. Have them trace Figure 8-1 with a finger.
Common error: using partial carb heat or turning it off when the engine runs rough as ice melts. Stress full heat until power returns.
Have the student explain the ammeter and low-voltage light in your airplane, and show which circuit breakers protect what.
Examiners like to ask about the magneto check and why 'no drop' is a no-go, and what an ignition switch left on can do to someone moving the prop.
For glass airplanes, have the student show how a nav source change affects the autopilot mode, and practice hand-flying with the autopilot off.
Drill the alternate static source effects and the blocked pitot vs static table; they are classic oral questions.
gaps: Exact limits (mag drop, vacuum range, oil pressure/temperature, fuel capacity, flap speeds, battery and electrical loads, emergency procedures) are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM of the airplane used for the checkride.

Specific avionics and autopilot operation (modes, buttons, failure displays) depends on the installed equipment; use the manufacturer's guide. AFH notes glass-display failure indications are not standardized. [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]

activities.title: Move it and see what happens
activities.intro: Tap a control input, then what it does.

pairs.r: Right aileron up, left aileron down, airplane rolls right
Elevator trailing edge goes up, tail down, nose up
Rudder moves left and the nose yaws left
Elevator trim tab moves to its full up position
More camber and lift, lots of drag, nose-down pitch
Slides back on tracks, adding wing area and camber

activities.title: Carb ice: what happens next?
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the events in order, then tap Check.
steps: In cruise with a fixed-pitch prop, RPM slowly drops
You pull carburetor heat to full hot
RPM drops a little more and the engine may run rough
RPM slowly rises as the ice melts
Normal power returns, so the ice is gone

activities.title: Pitot, static or alternate?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Airspeed drops to zero, drain hole still open
Only the airspeed indicator is affected
VSI stays at zero while you climb
Airspeed reads low as you climb above the altitude where it happened
Altimeter reads slightly higher than actual
VSI shows a short climb, then settles

activities.title: True or false: when systems fail

cards.s: Most in-flight electrical failures are in the alternator or generator.
cards.why: Yes. Once it goes off line, the battery is the only electrical source in a typical light airplane [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

cards.s: After an alternator failure, the battery will run everything for at least an hour.
cards.why: No. A 40-amp load might drain the battery in about 10 or 15 minutes. Shed non-essential loads right away [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

cards.s: Electric flaps are fine to use on a weak battery because flap motors use little power.
cards.why: No. Gear and flap motors use power much faster than most equipment and can cause a total loss of electrical power [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

cards.s: The first sign of an electrical fire is usually the smell of burning insulation.
cards.why: Yes. Then try to find and isolate the bad circuit, and land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

cards.s: With a split flap, the airplane rolls toward the wing with less flap.
cards.why: Yes. Counter it with opposite aileron and rudder, and fly the approach faster than normal [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

cards.s: A partly blocked static port always shows up right after takeoff.
cards.why: No. The instruments may work normally in the climb and cruise, and the problem may not show until you descend [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

final_quiz.q: You roll into a left turn with aileron only and no rudder. Which way does the nose start to yaw?
options: Left, but only at high airspeed
final_quiz.why: That is adverse yaw. The down aileron on the right wing makes more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws right, opposite the bank. Left rudder fixes it. [[1:151|PHAK 6-3]] [[1:152|PHAK 6-4]]

final_quiz.q: Using the chart, which day has the highest risk of carburetor ice?
final_quiz.why: Carb ice is most likely below 70 °F (21 °C) with humidity above 80%. The other days are still possible, just less likely. [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]] [[1:170|PHAK Fig 7-12]]

final_quiz.q: You are about to start a long, power-off descent on a cool, humid day in a carbureted airplane. When should you apply carb heat?
options: After you level off at the new altitude
Never at low power, since carb heat is for takeoff
Only if the engine starts to run rough
final_quiz.why: Carb ice is most dangerous at reduced power and can build unnoticed until you add power. Put the heat full on before closing the throttle and leave it on. [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]

final_quiz.q: In a long, slow climb on a hot day, the cylinder head temperature nears the red line. What helps cool the engine?
options: Lean the mixture and keep the steep climb
Lower the nose for more airspeed and enrich the mixture
Add power to climb out of the heat faster
final_quiz.why: To bring CHT down, increase airspeed, enrich the mixture and/or reduce power. Cowl flaps should be opened, not closed, when the engine is hot. [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]

final_quiz.q: Your fuel sample from a tank that should hold 100LL is clear with no color and smells like kerosene. What fuel is probably in the tank?
final_quiz.why: Jet A is colorless or straw colored and smells like kerosene. 100LL is dyed blue, 100 green and 80 red. [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]

final_quiz.q: In flight, you switch the ALT half of the split master switch OFF. What happens?
options: The engine quits because the magnetos lose power
The alternator keeps charging the battery
The battery now carries the whole electrical load
final_quiz.why: With the alternator side off, the entire load is on the battery, so turn off nonessential equipment. The magnetos don't need the electrical system. [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]] [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]

final_quiz.q: Ice blocks both the pitot opening and its drain hole, but the static port is clear. You hold the same airspeed and climb. What does the airspeed indicator show?
final_quiz.why: The pitot pressure is trapped. As static pressure falls in the climb, the airspeed reads higher, so it acts like an altimeter. It drops to zero only when the drain hole stays open. [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]

final_quiz.q: On a winter flight with the cabin heat on, your passenger gets a headache and feels drowsy. You smell no exhaust. What should you do?
options: Keep the heat on, since no smell means no CO
Climb higher to find fresher air
Turn the heater off, open the fresh air vents and use oxygen if you have it
Turn the heat up to keep the passenger awake
final_quiz.why: CO can be present in dangerous amounts even with no exhaust smell. Headache and drowsiness are CO signs: heater off, fresh air vents and windows open, oxygen if available. [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]

final_quiz.q: You will cruise at a cabin altitude of 14,500 feet MSL for 20 minutes. What does 14 CFR 91.211 require?
options: The required flight crew must use oxygen the whole time above 14,000 feet
Only that passengers be provided with oxygen
Oxygen use only after the first 30 minutes
Nothing, because the time is under 30 minutes
final_quiz.why: Above 14,000 feet MSL, the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen for the entire time at those altitudes. The 30-minute allowance is only for above 12,500 up to 14,000 feet. Passengers must be provided oxygen only above 15,000 feet. [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]

final_quiz.q: Your electric flaps won't extend before landing. What should you plan for?
options: A lower nose attitude on final than normal
A steep dive on final to lose altitude
A shorter landing roll than normal
More runway and a wider, longer pattern
final_quiz.why: A no-flap landing can need up to 50 percent more landing distance. A wider, longer pattern keeps you from diving and building up speed, and the nose sits higher than normal. [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]

final_quiz.q: You fly a glass-cockpit trainer with the autopilot on. Which habit best manages automation risk?
options: Watch it less once it is engaged, since reliable systems rarely fail
Leave the autopilot on even when it does something unexpected
Know which modes are engaged and armed, and check that armed modes engage
Check the autopilot only at the end of each leg
final_quiz.why: Always know which modes are engaged and armed, and verify armed modes engage. Humans watch reliable automation poorly. If it misbehaves, disengage it and fly by hand. [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]

final_quiz.q: After shutdown, a student turns the master switch OFF but leaves the ignition on BOTH. Why is that dangerous?
options: The engine could fire if someone moves the propeller
The electric fuel pump will keep running
final_quiz.why: Magnetos make their own electricity. With the ignition left on, moving the prop can start the engine even with the master off. [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]

final_quiz.q: According to the AFH, which is an acceptable way to use a checklist?
options: Do the items, then use the checklist to confirm they are all done
Stop using it once you know the airplane well
Use it only on the first flight of the day
final_quiz.why: A checklist is a memory aid, not just a do list. You may do the actions first and then use it to check them. What matters is using it every time. [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]
